To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IGF-I receptor expression is increased and IGF-I expression is decreased in the chronically STZ-diabetic kidney, and the increase in IGH-I receptor mRNA is not associated with an increase in IGF-1 mRNA.

IGF-I and the IGF-I receptor are differentially regulated in the kidney of chronically hypoinsulinaemic rats and that IGF-I receptor expression may be important in the regulation of kidney blood flow in chronic diabetes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the expression of IGF-I and its receptor in the kidney in chronic diabetes and the role of these peptides in the pathophysiology of diabetic nephropathy.
the regulation of gene expression of IGF-I and the IGF-I receptor in the chronically hypo- and hyperinsulinemically rat kidney.
the regulation of the IGF system in diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the kidney IGF-I receptor is regulated in a glucose-dependent manner in the chronically hypo- or hyperinsulinemic diabetic state, and that renal IGF-I and renal IGF-I receptor are not regulated in parallel in chronic diabetes.
the kidney IGF-I receptor is regulated differently in the acute versus the chronic phase of diabetes.
the IGF-I system is involved in the regulation of renal hypertrophy and hyperperfusion, but not the cause of them, in STZ-induced diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IGF-I receptor expression is regulated by glucose levels, whereas IGF-1 expression is regulated by insulin levels in the kidney.
the IGF-I receptor is the key factor in the regulation of renal hypertrophy and hyperperfusion in the chronically hypo- or hyperinsulinemic state.
hyperperfusion in diabetes is not explained by the increase in IGH-I or its receptor, and is not related to the increase in renal mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IGF-I and its receptor are regulated in a different fashion in the diabetic kidney compared with other organs.
the kidney is a major target organ for IGF-I action, but it is not a major source of circulating IGF-I.

IGF-I and its receptor are important in mediating the effects of hyperglycemia in the diabetic kidney, and that IGF-I is not the main mediator of renal hyperperfusion in the chronically hyperglycemic kidney.
